# Education in China
Education in China has transformed dramatically since 1949, progressing from a focus on mass literacy to nine years of compulsory education covering nearly all the population. The education system is structured as six years of primary school, three years of junior middle school, and three years of senior high school, with compulsory education covering the first nine years. Since the 1980s, reforms have emphasized science, technology, and economic modernization, leading to increased funding, decentralization of education administration, and improved access. While core curricula include Chinese, mathematics, and a growing focus on political studies from an early age, vocational and technical schools also play a substantial role in secondary education. Enrollment in primary and lower secondary schools has reached near universality, and the gross enrollment rate for higher education climbed to 58.42% in 2020, making China’s higher education system the largest in the world with over 44 million students. China is recognized globally for its high academic performance, with students excelling in international competitions and leading OECD evaluations.
Despite these achievements, significant challenges remain. A pronounced gap exists in educational quality and access between urban and rural regions, and among marginalized groups, including migrant children and people with disabilities. Academic rigor, rote memorization, and high-stakes testing—exemplified by the gaokao university entrance exam—drive intense competition and associated stress. Reforms since 2018 have sought to reduce homework and private tutoring burdens. The state maintains strict control over curricula and textbooks, ensuring alignment with Communist Party principles and restricting foreign influence. Continued expansion of adult, private, supplemental, and international education reflects evolving demands, though disparities and issues like regional inequality, food safety, and academic censorship persist within the system.
